paper.title: Weight gain leads to greater adverse metabolic responses in South Asian compared with white European men: the GlasVEGAS study.

claims.finding: South Asians have a three- to fivefold higher prevalence of type 2 diabetes and develop the disease a decade earlier and at lower body mass index (BMI) values than white Europeans.
claims.quote: SAs have three- to fivefold higher type 2 diabetes prevalence, and develop the disease a decade earlier and at lower body mass index (BMI) values, than WEs1.

claims.finding: Weight gain interventions resulted in similar relative weight increases between ethnic groups, with white European men gaining 6.3% ± 0.2% and South Asian men gaining 6.5% ± 0.3% of total body weight (P = 0.62).
claims.quote: Increases in weight and BMI with the weight gain intervention were similar between groups, with the WE men gaining 6.3% ± 0.2% and SA men gaining 6.5% ± 0.3% in body weight in response to the intervention (P = 0.62 for ethnic difference).

claims.finding: In response to weight gain, insulin sensitivity measured by the Matsuda index dropped by 38% in South Asian men, compared to a 7% decrease in white European men (P = 0.02).
claims.quote: Insulin sensitivity, as assessed by the Matsuda insulin sensitivity index, decreased by 38% in SAs, but only by 7% in the WEs, in response to weight gain (P = 0.02 for ethnicity × weight gain interaction).

claims.finding: Fasting insulin levels increased by 175% in South Asian men after weight gain, whereas white European men showed no increase (P = 0.02).
claims.quote: Fasting insulin increased by 175% in SAs, compared to no increase in the WEs (P = 0.02 for ethnicity × weight gain interaction).

claims.finding: Insulin resistance measured by HOMAIR increased by 160% in South Asian men following weight gain compared to 4% in white European men (P = 0.01).
claims.quote: Similarly, HOMAIR increased by 160% in SAs compared with 4% in WEs (P = 0.01 for ethnicity × weight gain interaction).

claims.finding: White European men gained more than three times as much lean tissue as South Asian men during the weight gain phase (2.4 l versus 0.7 l).
claims.quote: It is, however, noteworthy that the WE men experienced a more than threefold larger increase in lean tissue in response to weight gain than SA men (2.4 l versus 0.7 l).

claims.finding: At baseline, postprandial insulin concentrations were 62% higher in South Asian men than white European men (P = 0.006), despite similar baseline glucose and fasting insulin levels.
claims.quote: Baseline postprandial insulin concentrations were 62% (P = 0.006) higher in SAs than WEs, although fasting glucose and insulin concentrations, and postprandial glucose concentrations, did not differ significantly at baseline between the ethnic groups.

claims.finding: South Asian participants had an 18% larger mean fat cell diameter (P = 0.006) and 76% larger fat cell volume (P = 0.006) at baseline than white European participants.
claims.quote: At baseline, mean adipocyte diameter (by 18%, P = 0.006) and adipocyte volume (by 76%, P = 0.006) were larger in SA participants.

claims.finding: At baseline, 60% of total fat cell volume in South Asian participants was contained in large adipocytes compared with 28% in white European participants (P = 0.01).
claims.quote: In SAs, 60% of their total adipocyte volume was contained in large adipocytes compared with 28% in WEs (P = 0.01).

claims.finding: Cardiorespiratory fitness (maximal oxygen uptake) at baseline was 24% lower in absolute terms (P < 0.0001) and 14% lower relative to body weight (P = 0.0001) in South Asian participants compared with white European participants.
claims.quote: At baseline, maximal oxygen uptake was lower in SA than WE participants both in absolute terms (l min−1; 24% lower, P < 0.0001) and relative to body weight (ml kg−1 min−1; 14% lower, P = 0.0001).

claims.finding: Data following the weight loss phase could not be reliably presented because only 3 South Asian and 16 white European participants completed post-weight-loss measurements.
claims.quote: Only 3 SA and 16 WE participants completed measurements following the weight loss phase of the study; therefore, these data are not robust and have not been presented.

claims.finding: The study findings are limited by being conducted exclusively in young, lean men.
claims.quote: The study was also limited to young, lean men, who we chose as the participant group in this initial study for two main reasons.

draft.message: South Asian biology responds differently to weight gain, showing sharper drops in insulin sensitivity, which is why metabolic care must be personalized and doctor-led.
draft.reasoning: This message addresses the audience's frustration with standard diet advice by grounding their experience in biology rather than personal failure. By highlighting metabolic differences documented in clinical research, it reinforces the need for personalized doctor-led plans built on blood work.

draft.caption:
Ever wondered why standard diet advice does not work the same for everyone? Research shows that in response to weight gain, insulin sensitivity dropped by 38% in South Asian men, compared to a 7% decrease in white European men. In the same trial, fasting insulin levels increased by 175% in South Asian men. This study was conducted exclusively in young, lean men, showing why personalized labs matter. At Steer, our doctors screen your blood tests to build a personalized metabolic plan made for Indian lifestyles. Before you start, hear it from a doctor, not a reel.
